title: The Solar Car Race
sum: Three sixth graders build a tiny solar car for the class Solar Sprint and find out, one problem at a time, what its panel really needs.

cast.d: eleven, the team's note-keeper, who writes down every number
cast.look: an eleven-year-old girl with a long brown braid, round glasses, a green hoodie and a pencil behind her ear

cast.d: eleven, loud and fast, who tries things first and thinks second
cast.look: an eleven-year-old boy with short black hair, a bright orange T-shirt and scuffed white sneakers

cast.d: eleven, quiet and good with wires, with a dry sense of humor
cast.look: an eleven-year-old boy with close-cropped hair and dark brown skin, a blue striped polo shirt and a black digital watch

cast.d: the sixth-grade science teacher who runs the Solar Sprint
cast.look: a woman in her forties with short curly black hair, a denim shirt, a coffee mug and a stopwatch on a red cord

cast.d: eleven, captain of Blue Streak, the friendly rival team
cast.look: an eleven-year-old girl with a long black ponytail and a blue baseball cap
a shoebox-sized white foam-board car with a dark blue solar panel on top, four small black wheels, red and black clip wires and a masking-tape name label

p: On Monday, Ms. Alvarez set a small cardboard box on every table in Room 12. Then she wrote two words across the whiteboard in enormous capital letters: SOLAR SPRINT. “The Friday after next,” she said. “Every team will build a car that runs on sunlight, with no batteries, no pushing and no parents doing the work.”

The race would take place on the blacktop behind the gymnasium, along a lane exactly ten meters long. Every team also had to write a report full of real measurements. “A car without a report,” said Ms. Alvarez, “is only an expensive toy.” Dev had the box open before she finished talking, and he tipped everything out in front of Nora and Kofi with a clatter.

Nora read the parts list aloud while Kofi sorted the pieces into neat rows on the table. There was one solar panel, one electric motor about the size of her thumb, four plastic wheels and two metal axles. Last came a red wire and a black wire, each with a tiny metal clip at both ends.

The panel was the most interesting part, a rectangle of dark blue glass crossed by thin silver lines like a map of tiny streets. Kofi measured it with his ruler, 10 centimeters along one side and 12 centimeters along the other. Nora copied both measurements into the report notebook. Underneath them she wrote Area and drew a blank line to fill in later.

Meanwhile, Dev had already cut the body of the car out of white foam board. It was only 8 centimeters wide, so when he balanced the panel on top, it hung over both edges like a hat two sizes too big. “It looks like a mushroom,” said Kofi. Dev cut a wider body without another word about mushrooms.

By the end of the period, they had something that looked like a car. The motor sat at the back, with its tiny gear pressed against a larger gear on the axle. Dev connected the red wire from the panel to the motor and set the car on the floor. Absolutely nothing happened, even when he poked the motor with his finger.

“It's broken,” Dev said. “They gave us the broken one.” Kofi traced the wires with his finger, from the panel to the motor and back again. The black wire was attached to the panel, but its other clip was dangling in the air. “It has to go all the way around,” Kofi said. “Out of the panel, through the motor and back to the panel, and we only did half.”

As soon as Kofi clipped on the black wire, a thin hum came from the back of the car, and the little gear began to turn. It turned, stopped and turned again, as if it could not make up its mind. “It's going like a sleepy snail,” said Dev, lying flat on the floor to watch.

Ms. Alvarez walked past with her coffee mug and glanced up at the ceiling lights. “Those are for reading,” she said. “Try the real thing.” So they carried the car outside, with Kofi holding the wires steady. The moment the sunshine hit the panel, the motor whined like a mosquito and the wheels spun so fast they blurred.

Dev set the car down on the blacktop. Immediately it shot off, straight backward, until it bumped into his sneaker. Nora laughed so hard that she had to sit down on the steps. Dev looked at his shoe and then at the car, which was still trying to drive through it.

Kofi unclipped both wires from the motor and swapped them, and now the wheels spun in the opposite direction. “Swap the wires, swap the direction,” he said, as if he had known it all along. Nora wrote that in the report too.
This time the car rolled forward across the blacktop and stopped against the shoes of Ms. Alvarez, who had followed them outside. She studied it for a long moment. “It needs a name,” she said.

Dev wanted Lightning Bolt 3000, and Nora wanted Photon, which was a real science word. Kofi turned the car so that the panel faced the sky. “Sunny Side Up,” he said. “It only works one way.” Nora printed SUNNY SIDE UP on a strip of masking tape, and Dev stuck it across the front, slightly crooked.

art.s: On a sunny school blacktop, a small white foam-board solar car drives backward into a boy's white sneaker while a girl with a braid laughs on the gym steps and a quiet boy holds two clip wires.

q.q: Draw the panel, the two wires and the motor the way Kofi fixed them. Show where the light comes from.
look: one full loop from the panel to the motor and back to the panel
both wires clipped at both ends
the sun shining on the panel
q.e: That full loop is what Kofi traced with his finger. No loop, no hum!

q.q: Under the classroom lights, Dev said the gear was going “like a sleepy snail.” What did he mean?
c: It turned very fast.
It turned the wrong way.
It turned very slowly.
It turned with a loud buzz.
q.e: Snails are slow, and a sleepy one is even slower. The gear was barely moving.

q.q: Kofi measured the panel: 10 centimeters by 12 centimeters. What is its area? Tell how you worked it out.
q.a: 120 square centimeters. The panel is a rectangle, so I multiplied 10 by 12.
q.e: Ten rows of 12 little squares make 120 square centimeters.

p: On Tuesday, Ms. Alvarez unrolled a long measuring tape across the blacktop behind the gymnasium. Kofi held the zero end on the start line while she walked the other end past the basketball hoop. At exactly 10 meters, she knelt and chalked a thick white line, and beside it she printed FINISH. “Test runs, ten minutes for each team,” she said, holding up a stopwatch.

Nora had drawn a table in the report notebook the night before, with three columns labeled Run, Sky and Time. Dev leaned over her shoulder to inspect it. “You should add a column called Fastest Car Ever,” he said. Nora clicked her pen. “We only write down what we measure.”

The sky was bright and nearly empty, except for one fat white cloud that sat far away above the gym roof, not doing much of anything. Kofi positioned Sunny Side Up behind the start line with its panel facing the sun. When Ms. Alvarez said “Go,” he let go.

The motor whined, and the car took off down the lane. It traveled a little crooked but kept going, past the basketball hoop and over a crack in the blacktop shaped like a lightning bolt. Dev ran beside it the whole way, shouting its name. When the front wheels crossed the chalk, Ms. Alvarez stopped the clock and turned it around so everybody could read the display: 8.0 seconds.

Nora recorded Run 1, sunny, 8.0 in her table while Kofi carried the car back for a second try. Nobody was paying attention to the fat white cloud anymore. It had drifted over the gym while they were celebrating, and just as Kofi let go, its shadow slid across the lane like a gray blanket.

The car started quickly, but then the whine of the motor sank lower and lower, like a music box winding down. Sunny Side Up slowed to a crawl, crept past the lightning-bolt crack and stopped in the middle of the lane. Dev crouched beside it and begged it to keep going, but the wheels refused to budge.

Kofi walked the measuring tape out to the car, which had stopped at the 4-meter mark. “Four out of ten,” said Nora, writing it down, and Dev groaned because that was not even halfway. Kofi tilted his head and considered the tape for a moment. “Two out of every five,” he said, “which sounds a lot better.”

Then the far edge of the shadow slid off the lane. Sunlight hit the panel, and Sunny Side Up woke up all by itself, whining and wobbling toward the finish with nobody touching it. Dev chased it the rest of the way, yelling, “It's alive!”

“That one doesn't count,” said Ms. Alvarez, although she was laughing. Kofi picked up the car and held it so that the wheels spun freely in the air. When he cupped his hand over the panel, the whine dropped low, exactly the way it had under the cloud. As soon as he took his hand away, the wheels blurred again. “Less light in, less electricity out,” he said, “so a cloud is just an enormous hand.”

Back inside, Dev wanted to write the report himself. “Put down that our car is incredibly fast and clouds are the worst,” he said. Nora wrote something different in her tidiest handwriting. Under Claim, she wrote that Sunny Side Up needed full sunlight. Under Evidence, she listed both runs: Run 1 was sunny and took 8.0 seconds, and Run 2 was cloudy and stopped at 4 meters.
“Mine was more exciting,” said Dev, after reading the page twice. “Mine was true,” said Nora, but she let him draw a small cloud next to Run 2, and Dev gave it an extremely angry face.

art.s: A gray cloud shadow slides across a chalk race lane behind a school gym, where a tiny solar car has stopped halfway while a boy crouches beside it and a girl with a braid writes in a notebook.

q.q: The car stopped at 4 meters on the 10-meter lane. Draw the lane as 10 equal boxes and color how far it got. Then draw it as 5 equal boxes. How many do you color now?
look: a lane of 10 equal boxes with 4 colored
the same lane in 5 equal boxes with 2 colored
the colored part is the same length both times
q.e: 4 out of 10 and 2 out of 5 cover the same stretch of lane. Kofi was right. It does sound better!

q.q: Why did Sunny Side Up slow down and stop when the cloud came over?
q.a: The cloud blocked some of the sunlight. With less light on the panel, it made less electricity, so the motor slowed down and stopped.
q.e: Kofi's hand showed the same thing: less light in, less electricity out.

q.q: Nora's report had a claim and then evidence. Which sentence is evidence?
c: Our car is super fast.
Clouds are the worst.
Our car will win the race.
Run 1 was sunny and took 8.0 seconds.
q.e: Evidence is something you measured or saw. The stopwatch said 8.0 seconds, so that one is evidence.

p: On Wednesday, Dev arrived at school with a plastic dump truck tucked under his arm. It belonged to his little sister, and he had asked her permission first. Mostly. Before Nora had even unzipped her backpack, Dev had borrowed the truck's back wheels and attached them to Sunny Side Up. They were twice as big as the original wheels from the kit.

He had made one more improvement. Underneath the back edge of the panel, he had taped a pink eraser cut into a wedge, so the panel tilted upward like a beach chair. “Big wheels for speed,” he said, “and the wedge because real race cars lean.” Kofi opened his mouth to say something, then decided to close it again.

Out on the blacktop, the afternoon sun hung low above the gymnasium. Kofi positioned the car at the start line, and this time Sunny Side Up did not wobble or hesitate. It zipped down the lane and crossed the chalk in a little over 6 seconds, faster than it had ever traveled before. Dev threw both arms in the air and yelled, “Big wheels!”

Nora did not throw her arms anywhere. Instead, she frowned at the car and tapped her pen against the notebook, exactly the way she did during math tests. “Was it the wheels or the wedge?” Dev patted the big wheels as if they were a pair of prize-winning puppies. “Both, obviously.”

“I can't write obviously in a science report,” said Nora. “Then write that Dev is a genius,” said Dev, grinning at his own idea. Kofi crouched beside the car and examined it for a while. “We changed two things at the same time,” he said, “so now we can't possibly tell which one made the difference.”

Kofi's plan was simple, but it would take longer. First they would put the small wheels back and keep the wedge, so that only one thing was different from before. After that, they would test the big wheels with the panel lying flat. Ms. Alvarez held up three fingers and said, “Three runs for every experiment, because one run can be luck.”

Dev groaned, but he removed the big wheels, and Kofi raced the car three times in a row with the small wheels and the wedge. The stopwatch said 6.1, then 5.8, then 6.1. Nora recorded the times in a neat column and added them up, tapping each decimal point with her pencil. When she divided the total by three, the average was a nice round number, just as fast as Dev's first run.

Next came the big wheels with the panel lying flat again. Dev reattached the wheels and removed the wedge, muttering the whole time. All three runs took about 8 seconds, which was no faster than Tuesday's sunny run. Dev stared at the enormous wheels in disbelief. “So my wheels did nothing?” “They look fantastic,” said Kofi.

Back in Room 12, Kofi borrowed a flashlight from the supply shelf. When he pointed it straight down at the table, it made a small, bright circle. Then he tilted the flashlight sideways, and the circle stretched into a long, pale oval. “It's the same amount of light,” he said, “just spread out thinner.”

Nora glanced at the window, where the afternoon sunshine was slanting across the desks. “So a flat panel only gets the thin, stretched-out light,” she said, “and the wedge aims it directly at the sun.” Kofi switched off the flashlight and turned to Dev. “Also, real race cars don't lean.”

The next morning, Dev read the report over Nora's shoulder. Under Test 2 she had written: Big wheels, flat panel, no faster. “That's harsh,” said Dev, so Nora added one more line underneath: Dev says the big wheels look better, and Kofi agrees.
That afternoon, the big wheels went back on his sister's truck, but the pink eraser remained. Dev taped it down twice as tightly and wrote THE WEDGE on its side in black permanent marker.

art.s: In a classroom, a boy tilts a flashlight so its light makes a long pale oval on a table, while two classmates watch beside a small solar car with a pink eraser wedge under its panel and a toy dump truck missing its back wheels.

q.q: With the small wheels and the wedge, the three times were 6.1, 5.8 and 6.1 seconds. What was the average time? Show how you know.
q.e: Put the three runs together to get 18 seconds, then share them out evenly. Each run gets 6.

q.q: Draw Dev and Nora right after the first fast run. Give each of them a speech bubble that shows what they think made the car faster.
look: Dev's bubble says the big wheels did it, or both
Nora's bubble asks if it was the wheels or the wedge
faces that show two different feelings
q.e: Two people, two points of view. Your bubbles show both!

q.q: Kofi put the small wheels back but kept the wedge. Why?
c: So the car would weigh less
So only one thing was different
So the car would look better
So the wheels would last longer
q.e: When you change one thing at a time, you know which change made the difference.

p: The day before the Solar Sprint, the fifth graders organized a bake sale in the front hallway. Dev bought a strawberry jam donut for a dollar and devoured it on the way to science. By the time he reached Room 12, there was powdered sugar down his shirt and a spot of jam on his chin. He grabbed Sunny Side Up off the shelf and hurried outside.

The sky was as blue as a swimming pool, without a single cloud anywhere. Kofi checked THE WEDGE, positioned the car at the start line and let go. Sunny Side Up hummed down the lane, and at the finish Ms. Alvarez stopped the clock and frowned at the display, which read 7.4 seconds.

Nora could hardly believe it, because last week the car had averaged about 6 seconds with the wedge. She wrote 7.4 in the table and subtracted in the margin. “We're more than a second slower,” she said, “on a better day.” Dev flung his arms toward the empty sky. “There's nothing even blocking it!”

They inspected everything, one piece at a time. Kofi pinched both clips on the motor, and both were perfectly tight. The wedge was still in position, and the wheels spun freely when Nora flicked them. Then Kofi tipped the panel toward the light and went very still.

In one corner of the blue glass was a pink, shiny smear, and right in the middle of it was a fingerprint. Everybody turned to look at Dev, and Dev looked at his thumb, which was still a little sticky. “That,” he said, “might possibly be jam.”

Nora measured the smear with her ruler, and it was about 3 centimeters by 4 centimeters. She flipped back to the first page of the report, where the panel's measurements were written down. The panel was 10 centimeters by 12 centimeters, or 120 square centimeters altogether.

“It's only a tiny patch, so it can't possibly matter that much,” said Dev. Kofi pointed at the stopwatch. “It mattered 1.4 seconds.” Before anyone could stop him, Dev grabbed the bottom of his T-shirt and rubbed the panel hard.
The smear refused to come off. Instead, it spread into a wide pink streak twice as big as before, and the glass felt tacky under his fingers. “Great,” said Nora, “now it's a pink cloud.”

“Jam is mostly sugar, and you can't rub sugar off,” Kofi said. “You have to dissolve it.” He was remembering his grandmother's tea, where two spoonfuls of sugar disappeared completely as soon as she stirred, especially when the tea was still hot.
Ms. Alvarez had already gone inside, and she returned with a paper cup of warm water and a soft cloth. “Use warm water, not hot,” she said, “and dab it instead of scrubbing.”

Nora dipped the cloth and pressed it against the streak. The pink faded to a faint blush and then vanished altogether. When she squeezed the cloth out over the grass, the drips were pale pink and slightly sticky, because the jam had gone into the water. Kofi dried the glass with a clean corner of the cloth, and the silver lines sparkled again.

When Kofi raced the car one more time, it whined down the lane and crossed the chalk in 6.0 seconds, right where it belonged. Dev let out a breath so enormous that his cheeks puffed out. “Sorry, Sunny,” he said, patting the foam with one clean finger.

Back inside, Nora wrote a notice on an index card in thick black marker. NOTICE: No food within one meter of Sunny Side Up. Wash your hands first. This means you, Dev. She taped it to the lid of the car's box. By the end of the day, a second line had appeared underneath in Dev's messy handwriting: Donuts allowed AFTER the race.

art.s: On a sunny school blacktop, a girl with a braid dabs a pink jam smear off a small solar panel with a wet cloth while a boy with powdered sugar on his orange shirt stares at his sticky thumb.

q.q: Draw the notice Nora taped to the car's box. Show what it says and who it is really for.
look: a short, clear rule about food or clean hands
Dev's extra line at the bottom
q.e: A good notice is short and clear. Nora's even had a joke in it!

q.q: Dev's shirt only smeared the jam, but warm water cleaned it off. Why did the water work?
q.a: Jam is mostly sugar, and sugar dissolves in water. The water mixed with the jam and carried it away, so the cloth could wipe it off.
q.e: The pink drips from the cloth showed it: the jam had gone into the water.

q.q: The jam covered 3 cm by 4 cm of a panel that was 120 square centimeters. What percent of the panel was covered?
q.e: 3 × 4 = 12 square centimeters. 12 out of 120 is 1 out of 10, and that is 10%.

p: On Friday, the entire sixth grade gathered on the blacktop, along with several parents who were holding up their phones to record videos. The chalk lane had been redrawn, bright and thick, with START at one end and FINISH ten meters away. Six solar cars waited in a row on the gym steps. The sky was mostly blue, but a stiff breeze was pushing puffy white clouds across it, like sheep that someone was hurrying along.

“One run each,” said Ms. Alvarez. “When I call your team, you have two minutes to start, and you can use them however you like.” She was studying the sky when she said the last part. Nora polished the panel one final time with a clean cloth, and Dev kept both hands safely in his pockets.

Priya's team competed right before them. Their car was called Blue Streak, and it had a paper lightning bolt decorating each side. It shot off the line, but halfway down the lane a cloud slid over the sun. Blue Streak slowed, crept forward and stopped at the 7-meter mark, and Priya pulled her cap down over her eyes and groaned.

When their turn came and the two minutes began, the same shadow still stretched across the entire lane. Dev grabbed the car and hurried toward the start line. “We have to go right now!” Kofi, however, was gazing past the lane at the soccer field.

Out on the field, the far edge of the shadow was moving. Behind it, the grass was bright green again, and the sunny part was sliding steadily toward them. “The wind is pushing the cloud along,” Kofi said, “so its shadow travels too.” Nora watched the bright edge cross the goalposts, then the long-jump pit, then the fence. Their teacher tapped her stopwatch. “One minute left!”

The sunlight swept across the blacktop like a tide coming in, reaching the finish line first and then Kofi's sneakers. In Dev's hands the motor began to whine, and Kofi said, “Now.” Dev set the car behind the start line with the wedge up and the panel pointed at the sun, and he let go.

Sunny Side Up traveled straighter than it had ever traveled before. It hummed past the basketball hoop and over the lightning-bolt crack while half the class chanted its name and several parents applauded. When it finally crossed the finish line, the stopwatch said 5.0 seconds.
Then Ms. Alvarez turned to Priya. “You got a cloud,” she said, “so run again while the sun is out.” This time Priya's car flew down the lane, and the stopwatch said 5.2.
Priya walked over and shook hands with Dev, then Kofi, then Nora. “Two tenths of a second,” she said, “and next year we're definitely bringing a wedge.”

The report still needed two more things before it was complete. The rule sheet asked for each car's speed in meters per second. Nora wrote 10 meters and 5.0 seconds at the top of a clean page, and Dev started counting by fives on his fingers. Before he had finished, Kofi had already written the answer in.

The last page needed a final sentence. Dev wanted WE WON in letters as tall as the page, and Nora wanted one more Claim and Evidence. Kofi took the pencil and wrote one quiet line underneath everything else: The sun did the driving. We just pointed the way.

That afternoon, Sunny Side Up sat on the windowsill of Room 12 with its panel facing up, soaking in the last of the afternoon light. Its masking-tape name was beginning to curl at one end. On Ms. Alvarez's desk, well over one meter away, sat a strawberry jam donut with Dev's name on it.

art.s: On race day, a class cheers along a chalk lane as a small solar car with a pink wedge under its panel speeds toward the finish, while the edge of a cloud shadow slides away across a soccer field under a blue sky with puffy clouds.

q.q: Kofi wrote, “The sun did the driving. We just pointed the way.” What did he mean?
q.a: The sunlight gave the car all its power, so in a way the sun made it go. The team only aimed the panel at the sun and kept everything working.
q.e: Kofi painted a picture with words. The sun can't really drive, but it was the car's only power.

q.q: Sunny Side Up went 10 meters in 5.0 seconds. How far did it go each second?
c: 0.5 meters
2 meters
5 meters
15 meters
q.e: 10 meters shared out over 5 seconds is 2 meters every second.

q.q: Draw what Kofi saw on the soccer field. Show the cloud, its shadow on the ground and the sunny part coming back. Add an arrow for the wind.
look: a cloud with its shadow on the ground under it
sunny ground coming toward the lane
an arrow showing which way the wind pushed the cloud
q.e: You drew the weather moving, just the way Kofi watched it!

fin.q: Over two weeks, Sunny Side Up went from 8 seconds to 5. Name two things the team did that helped, and say why each one worked.
fin.a: They tilted the panel with the wedge so the sunlight hit it straight on. They also cleaned off the jam and waited for the cloud to pass, so the panel got all the light it could.
fin.e: Every fix gave the panel more light. More light in, more electricity out.

fin.q: Which sentence is the best summary of the whole story?
c: A team builds a solar car, learns what its panel needs and wins by waiting for the sun.
Dev eats a jam donut and gets the solar panel sticky.
Ms. Alvarez chalks a 10-meter lane and times each car.
A cloud stops Priya's car in the middle of the Solar Sprint.
fin.e: A summary tells the whole story in one short line. The other choices are true, but each is only one small part.
